newsitem.title: USA: Huang unlikely to testify in Senate hearing-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Huang unlikely to testify in Senate hearing-lawyer.

text.p: The lawyer representing former Democratic Party fund-raiser John Huang said it appeared unlikely his client would testify before a Senate panel investigating campaign finance scandals.

Attorney Ty Cobb, speaking on Fox New Channel's "Fox on Politics", said the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee apparently had no interest in offering immunity to Huang in exchange for his testimony.

Republicans are trying to show that while he worked at the Commerce Department, Huang may have betrayed U.S. secrets to his former employer, the Indonesian-based Lippo industrial conglomerate, which in turn could have passed them on to China.

Cobb said Mike Madigan, chief counsel for the panel, sent him a letter Tuesday suggesting that committee members would limit their questions on other issues if Huang agreed to testify voluntarily on any matters related to espionage.

Huang has denied spying for China or any foreign country, and has not requested immunity for any testimony on disclosure of classified information, agents of foreign governments, economic espionage, unlawful communications or receipt of classified information.
But Cobb said this latest Republican proposal was "a non-starter" due to legal issues involved. "The answer is you can't do it practically," he said.
"At this stage of the game, I read this letter to suggest that the majority has no interest in immunising Mr. Huang in the sense that it has historically been done in Congress," Cobb told Fox.
Asked if that meant Huang would not testify, pleading the Fifth Amendment, Cobb said, "I think that's become increasingly clear."

Huang, an Asian-American, worked at the Commerce Department from June 1994 to January 1996 before becoming a fund-raiser for the Democratic National Committee. He has refused to cooperate with the Senate investigation unless granted some form of immunity from prosecution.

Huang received secret briefings about China and visited the Chinese embassy and those of other Asian nations. He had access to classified State Department cables and saw up to 550 raw intelligence reports on China.
